---
title: "Generalized linear mixed models"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

So far, repeated response times have been modeled with a Gaussian conditional distribution. But the SuperTelicity response is binary: on each trial, a participant chose *in* or *for*. A Gaussian model could assign probabilities below zero or above one, so we need the [Bernoulli model](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) and its logit link.

A **generalized linear mixed model (GLMM)** combines that response model with [group deviations](random-intercepts.qmd). Thus it lets us model a binary response while still accounting for the fact that participants, verbs, and sentences recur.

The response [event](../foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd) is an *in* choice, and its [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) is the Bernoulli expected value. [Variance and covariance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) describe group variation, while conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) applies only after the shared deviations are supplied. Recall that a [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) holds the observed responses fixed and compares possible coefficient and variance values.

We first assemble those pieces with one participant intercept, then add the grouping structure in the recorded materials. Participants respond across sentence materials, while each sentence belongs to one verb. The model therefore combines a participant intercept with a verb--sentence hierarchy. The remaining question will be whether a prediction conditions on particular groups or averages over their fitted distributions.

We use cloze judgments from the [**SuperTelicity**](https://github.com/SuperMereo/supertelicity) study. On each trial, a participant selected *in* or *for*, a numeral, and a time unit for an event description. The preposition is a noisy behavioral measure related to telicity; habitual and other interpretations can also license a temporal modifier, so the choice does not directly reveal a semantic category. The [contentfulness classes](logistic-regression-with-multiple-predictors.qmd) compare lexically filled sentences, sentences with general nouns such as *person* and *thing*, and schematic *X verb Y* frames. Because the schematic frames occur only among episodic clauses, we fit the contentfulness comparison to episodic rows.

The analysis concerns the participants and trials represented in the table used below.

## Combining a Bernoulli response with group variation

Begin with one participant and one trial. Write $Y_i=1$ for an *in* response and $Y_i=0$ for a *for* response. The following summary selects an observed participant who used both responses and computes that participant's empirical proportion of *in* choices and its log odds.

```{r}
#| label: supertelicity-observed-participant-log-odds
supertelicity_preview <- read.csv(
  "data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv"
)
participant_probability <- tapply(
  supertelicity_preview$prep_in,
  supertelicity_preview$participant_id,
  mean
)
participant_trials <- table(supertelicity_preview$participant_id)
eligible_participants <- names(participant_probability)[
  participant_probability > 0 & participant_probability < 1
]
example_participant <- eligible_participants[[1L]]
observed_probability <- participant_probability[[example_participant]]
data.frame(
  participant_id = example_participant,
  trials = unname(participant_trials[[example_participant]]),
  empirical_in_probability = observed_probability,
  empirical_in_log_odds = qlogis(observed_probability)
)
```

The [logit link](logistic-regression.qmd) converts the observed proportion to log odds, which can range over the whole real line. We use this raw summary only to make the response and transformation concrete. The model probabilities come from the GLMM below, where a participant random intercept represents persistent movement on the log odds scale across that participant's trials.

Let $Y_i=1$ when trial $i$ has an *in* response. Conditional on the random effects,

$$
Y_i\mid u_{p[i]},v_{w[i]},s_{q[i]}
\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+u_{p[i]}+v_{w[i]}+s_{q[i]}.
$$

The vector $\mathbf x_i$ contains verb class, contentfulness, and their interaction. Participant $p$, verb $w$, and sentence $q$ receive independent random intercepts:

$$
u_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_p^2),\qquad
v_w\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_w^2),\qquad
s_q\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau_q^2).
$$

Conditional on these deviations, the Bernoulli likelihood is

$$
p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\pi)
=\prod_i \pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}.
$$

The inverse logit keeps every fitted value inside the probability interval. The random intercepts represent which rows share persistent participant, verb, or sentence tendencies.

The participant intercept accounts for repeated choices by a listener, the verb intercept for variation shared by all sentences built from that verb, and the sentence intercept for repeated judgments of one sentence. Participant identities cross the sentence materials: a participant contributes responses to many sentences, and sentences receive responses from many participants. Sentences are nested within verbs because every sentence identifier belongs to exactly one verb. We assume the three random intercept distributions are independent. This structure holds the verb type and contentfulness associations constant across participants and materials; a richer random slope model would allow those associations to vary.

## From the conditional model to the likelihood

The conditional likelihood above still contains the unobserved participant, verb,
and sentence deviations. We cannot maximize it as though those deviations were
additional population coefficients, because the model says that they are draws
from normal distributions. We instead combine the two parts of the model and
then average over every possible collection of deviations.

To write that calculation compactly, collect all participant, verb, and sentence
intercepts into one $d$-dimensional vector $\mathbf b$. Let $\mathbf z_i$ select
the three entries of $\mathbf b$ that belong to trial $i$. We can then rewrite
the fitted log odds, which we will call $m_i$, as

$$
m_i
=\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b,
\qquad
\pi_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(m_i).
$$

The vector $\boldsymbol\theta=(\tau_p,\tau_w,\tau_q)$ contains the three group
standard deviations. Under the independence assumptions above, the covariance
matrix $\mathbf G(\boldsymbol\theta)$ has participant variances, verb variances,
and sentence variances on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Thus

$$
\mathbf b
\sim
\mathcal N_d
\left(
\mathbf 0,
\mathbf G(\boldsymbol\theta)
\right).
$$

For fixed values of $\boldsymbol\beta$, $\boldsymbol\theta$, and $\mathbf b$, the
joint density of the observed responses and the possible group deviations is

$$
p(\mathbf y,\mathbf b
\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\left\{
\prod_i
\pi_i(\mathbf b)^{y_i}
[1-\pi_i(\mathbf b)]^{1-y_i}
\right\}
\phi_d
\left\{
\mathbf b;
\mathbf 0,
\mathbf G(\boldsymbol\theta)
\right},
$$

where $\phi_d$ is a $d$-dimensional normal density. The first factor asks how
well a particular collection of deviations predicts the observed choices. The
second asks how plausible that collection is under the proposed group
distributions. Their product prevents a group with a small number of trials
from receiving any deviation that happens to fit those trials perfectly.

The **marginal likelihood** averages this joint density over the deviations:

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf y)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
p(\mathbf y,\mathbf b
\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
\,d\mathbf b.
$$

This integral is the quantity we want to compare across candidate values of the
population coefficients and group standard deviations. It has one integration
dimension for every entry of $\mathbf b$, and the logistic inverse link usually
prevents us from evaluating it with ordinary algebra.

The [Laplace approximation](laplace-approximation.qmd) gives us a way forward.
For a particular candidate $(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)$, define the log
integrand

$$
h(\mathbf b;
\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\log p(\mathbf y,\mathbf b
\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
$$

and let $\widehat{\mathbf b}$ be the value that maximizes it. This is the
**conditional mode** for that candidate. We also need to know how rapidly the
log integrand bends downward around the mode. The matrix

$$
\mathbf H
=
-\left.
\frac{\partial^2 h(\mathbf b;
\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)}
{\partial\mathbf b\,\partial\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}}
\right|_{\mathbf b=\widehat{\mathbf b}}
$$

collects that local curvature. This matrix is a [Hessian](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature): its diagonal entries record curvature along individual random effect directions, while its off-diagonal entries record how two directions bend together. As in the [Gaussian mixed model likelihood](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd#gaussian-mixed-model-likelihood), the determinant $|\mathbf H|$ combines those directions into a measure of the peak's local volume.

The multivariate Laplace approximation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf y)
&\approx
\exp\left\{
h(\widehat{\mathbf b};
\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
\right\}
(2\pi)^{d/2}
|\mathbf H|^{-1/2},\\[4pt]
\log L(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf y)
&\approx
h(\widehat{\mathbf b};
\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)
+\frac d2\log(2\pi)
-\frac12\log|\mathbf H|.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both the height and the curvature matter. A candidate can produce a high joint
density at its best deviations but concentrate that density in such a narrow
region that its integrated likelihood is smaller than that of another
candidate.

The fitting calculation therefore has an inner and an outer problem. For each
candidate $(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)$, the inner calculation finds
$\widehat{\mathbf b}$ and $\mathbf H$, and then substitutes them into the
approximation above. The outer optimizer changes
$(\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\theta)$ and repeats the inner calculation until it
finds coefficient and variance values with the largest approximate marginal
likelihood. The resulting coefficients and standard deviations are therefore
approximate maximum likelihood estimates under the Laplace objective. They are
not exact maximizers of the integral written above. In `glmer()`, `nAGQ = 1`
requests this Laplace calculation with one approximation point;
`bobyqa` carries out the outer search. The value one refers to the approximation
point at the conditional mode. It does not refer to one observation or one
random effect.

## Fitting the participant and verb--sentence model

The function `glmer()` carries out the calculation we have just assembled. The formula names the binary response and three grouping units, while `family = binomial(link = "logit")` supplies the Bernoulli response model and logit link. We use [sum coding](sum-coding.qmd) for the categorical predictors: each contrast column sums to zero, so the intercept refers to the coding center and the verb coefficient represents one half of the signed two-level contrast. The setting `nAGQ = 1` requests the Laplace approximation, `bobyqa` names the outer numerical search algorithm, and `maxfun` sets its evaluation budget.

```{r}
#| label: fit-supertelicity-glmm
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

supertelicity_all <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
supertelicity <- subset(supertelicity_all, clause_type == "episodic")
supertelicity$participant_id <- factor(supertelicity$participant_id)
supertelicity$verb <- factor(supertelicity$verb)
supertelicity$sentence_id <- factor(supertelicity$sentence_id)
supertelicity$verb_type <- factor(
  supertelicity$verb_type,
  levels = c("manner", "result")
)
supertelicity$contentfulness <- factor(
  supertelicity$contentfulness,
  levels = c("contentful", "bleached", "templatic")
)

contrasts(supertelicity$verb_type) <- contr.sum(2)
contrasts(supertelicity$contentfulness) <- contr.sum(3)

fit <- glmer(
  prep_in ~ verb_type * contentfulness +
    (1 | participant_id) +
    (1 | verb) +
    (1 | sentence_id),
  data = supertelicity,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = glmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

scaled_gradient <- function(model) {
  gradient <- model@optinfo$derivs$gradient
  hessian <- model@optinfo$derivs$Hessian
  solve(chol(hessian), gradient)
}

fit_scaled_gradient <- scaled_gradient(fit)
fit_fixed_effect_covariance <- as.matrix(vcov(fit))
fit_diagnostics <- c(
  optimizer_code = fit@optinfo$conv$opt,
  convergence_messages = length(fit@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages),
  maximum_absolute_scaled_gradient = max(abs(fit_scaled_gradient)),
  smallest_fixed_effect_covariance_eigenvalue = min(eigen(
    fit_fixed_effect_covariance,
    symmetric = TRUE,
    only.values = TRUE
  )$values)
)

stopifnot(
  fit_diagnostics[["optimizer_code"]] == 0,
  fit_diagnostics[["convergence_messages"]] == 0,
  fit_diagnostics[["maximum_absolute_scaled_gradient"]] < 2e-3,
  fit_diagnostics[["smallest_fixed_effect_covariance_eigenvalue"]] > 0
)

fit_diagnostics

data_summary <- c(
  trials = nrow(supertelicity),
  participant_identifiers = nlevels(supertelicity$participant_id),
  verbs = nlevels(supertelicity$verb),
  sentences = nlevels(supertelicity$sentence_id),
  in_responses = sum(supertelicity$prep_in),
  for_responses = sum(1L - supertelicity$prep_in)
)
data_summary
```

The optimizer code and message count check whether the outer search reported a
failure. The scaled gradient asks a more direct question. A raw derivative can
look large merely because its parameter is measured on a different scale, so
the curvature matrix rescales the derivatives before we compare them with zero.
The reported maximum is below the usual `lme4` tolerance of $0.002$.

The covariance matrix returned by `vcov()` uses the inverse local curvature of
the approximate marginal objective near its optimum. Thus its diagonal entries
give local fixed effect variance estimates, and their square roots give the
reported standard errors. This calculation inherits both the local quadratic
approximation and the Laplace approximation used to construct the objective.
An eigenvalue here records the variance along one direction determined by the
coefficient covariance matrix. The positive smallest eigenvalue confirms that
every such direction has positive estimated variance; the inverse matrix
consequently has positive curvature in every fixed effect direction.

## Checking the Laplace approximation in a reduced model

The full model contains three crossed collections of random intercepts, so
high-order adaptive Gaussian quadrature is not available for that full
integral in `glmer()`. Adaptive quadrature replaces an integral with a weighted
sum of integrand values placed around its conditional mode; using more points
records more of the integrand's shape away from that mode. We can still check the approximation on the same binary
responses after retaining only the participant intercept. This reduced model
does not replace the scientific model above. It gives us a one-dimensional
integral for each participant, which `glmer()` can evaluate using either one
Laplace point or nine adaptive quadrature points.

```{r}
#| label: supertelicity-reduced-quadrature-check
reduced_formula <- prep_in ~ verb_type * contentfulness +
  (1 | participant_id)

reduced_laplace <- glmer(
  reduced_formula,
  data = supertelicity,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ = 1L,
  control = glmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

reduced_quadrature <- glmer(
  reduced_formula,
  data = supertelicity,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ = 9L,
  control = glmerControl(
    optimizer = "bobyqa",
    optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
  )
)

reduced_check <- data.frame(
  calculation = c("Laplace", "Nine-point adaptive quadrature"),
  log_likelihood = c(
    as.numeric(logLik(reduced_laplace)),
    as.numeric(logLik(reduced_quadrature))
  ),
  maximum_absolute_scaled_gradient = c(
    max(abs(scaled_gradient(reduced_laplace))),
    max(abs(scaled_gradient(reduced_quadrature)))
  ),
  optimizer_code = c(
    reduced_laplace@optinfo$conv$opt,
    reduced_quadrature@optinfo$conv$opt
  )
)

reduced_coefficient_difference <- max(abs(
  fixef(reduced_laplace) - fixef(reduced_quadrature)
))
reduced_standard_deviation_difference <- abs(
  attr(VarCorr(reduced_laplace)$participant_id, "stddev") -
    attr(VarCorr(reduced_quadrature)$participant_id, "stddev")
)

stopifnot(
  all(reduced_check$optimizer_code == 0),
  all(reduced_check$maximum_absolute_scaled_gradient < 2e-3),
  reduced_coefficient_difference < 0.01,
  reduced_standard_deviation_difference < 0.01
)

reduced_check
c(
  largest_fixed_effect_difference = reduced_coefficient_difference,
  participant_standard_deviation_difference =
    reduced_standard_deviation_difference
)
```

The two objective values need not be identical because one calculation keeps
more information about each one-dimensional integral. The fitted coefficients
and participant standard deviations are nevertheless close for this reduced
model. This agreement is evidence about the Laplace approximation on these
responses under the reduced grouping structure; it does not prove that the
three-way crossed approximation is exact.

One retained observation and the repetition counts make the unit structure visible:

```{r}
#| label: supertelicity-glmm-observation-and-repetition
#| echo: true
supertelicity[1L, c("participant_id", "verb", "sentence_id", "verb_type",
                    "contentfulness", "preposition", "prep_in")]
verbs_per_sentence <- aggregate(
  verb ~ sentence_id,
  data = supertelicity,
  FUN = function(x) length(unique(x))
)
sentences_per_verb <- table(unique(
  supertelicity[c("verb", "sentence_id")]
)$verb)
stopifnot(max(verbs_per_sentence$verb) == 1L)
c(participant_repetitions = max(table(supertelicity$participant_id)),
  verb_repetitions = max(table(supertelicity$verb)),
  sentence_repetitions = max(table(supertelicity$sentence_id)),
  minimum_sentences_per_verb = min(sentences_per_verb),
  maximum_sentences_per_verb = max(sentences_per_verb))
```

The incidence check confirms that each sentence belongs to one verb. The
sentence counts show how many distinct sentence materials contribute to each
verb intercept.

Sum coding assigns the two verb levels opposite signed values whose column sums are zero; the two contentfulness contrast columns compare the three levels around the coding center. Consequently, the printed `verb_type1` coefficient is one half of the manner-minus-result log odds contrast at the contentfulness coding center. The explicit `-2` transformation below changes its sign and doubles it to produce result minus manner.

The fitting settings govern numerical search. They do not alter the Bernoulli likelihood or compensate for missing random slopes.

We retain participant, verb, and sentence intercepts so that the marginal likelihood remains visible. The source analysis also includes participant, lexical, duration, list, and argument-form terms; its coefficients consequently answer a broader question.

## Raw sentence proportions and fitted probabilities

One raw point below is the proportion of *in* responses for one sentence. The fitted points set all three random intercepts to zero, so they describe a participant, verb, and sentence at the center of the fitted distributions on the log odds scale.

```{r}
#| label: plot-supertelicity-glmm
sentence_proportions <- aggregate(
  prep_in ~ verb_type + contentfulness + sentence_id,
  data = supertelicity,
  FUN = mean
)

prediction_grid <- expand.grid(
  verb_type = factor(
    c("manner", "result"),
    levels = levels(supertelicity$verb_type)
  ),
  contentfulness = factor(
    c("contentful", "bleached", "templatic"),
    levels = levels(supertelicity$contentfulness)
  )
)
prediction_grid$conditional_probability <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = prediction_grid,
  type = "response",
  re.form = NA
)

ggplot(
  sentence_proportions,
  aes(x = verb_type, y = prep_in)
) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.08,
    height = 0,
    shape = 1,
    size = 1.1,
    color = "grey55"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = prediction_grid,
    aes(y = conditional_probability),
    color = "#1F5A85",
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~contentfulness) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Verb class", y = "Probability of an in-response") +
  theme_classic()
```

With sum coding, the result-minus-manner contrast averaged over the contentfulness coding is

```{r}
#| label: supertelicity-verb-contrast
result_minus_manner_log_odds <- -2 * fixef(fit)[["verb_type1"]]
c(
  result_minus_manner_log_odds = result_minus_manner_log_odds,
  result_minus_manner_odds_ratio = exp(result_minus_manner_log_odds)
)
```

The interaction terms modify this comparison at particular contentfulness levels. The coefficient remains a conditional log-odds contrast: it compares trials with the same random effect values.

## Conditional and population-averaged prediction

A prediction at zero random effects is not generally the probability for a randomly drawn participant, verb, and sentence. Let $B$ be the sum of the three independent intercepts. Its variance is

$$
\tau_B^2=\tau_p^2+\tau_w^2+\tau_q^2.
$$

For a population log odds value $a$, the probability averaged over the random intercept distribution is

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\mathbf x)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a+b)
\phi(b;0,\tau_B^2)\,db.
$$

Here $\phi(b;0,\tau_B^2)$ is the normal density for a group deviation $b$ with mean zero and variance $\tau_B^2$. Multiplying by that density weights each possible deviation by how plausible it is under the fitted group distribution before the integral averages the resulting probabilities.

Because the inverse logit is nonlinear,

$$
\operatorname{E}_{B}
\left[\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a+B)\right]
\ne
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a)
$$

in general.

```{r}
#| label: plot-supertelicity-marginal
variance_components <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit))
total_random_variance <- sum(
  variance_components$vcov[is.na(variance_components$var2)]
)
population_location <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = prediction_grid,
  type = "link",
  re.form = NA
)

prediction_grid$marginal_probability <- vapply(
  population_location,
  function(a) {
    integrate(
      function(b) {
        plogis(a + b) *
          dnorm(b, sd = sqrt(total_random_variance))
      },
      lower = -Inf,
      upper = Inf,
      rel.tol = 1e-10
    )$value
  },
  numeric(1)
)

prediction_grid[1L, c("verb_type", "contentfulness",
                       "conditional_probability", "marginal_probability")]

ggplot(
  prediction_grid,
  aes(
    x = conditional_probability,
    y = marginal_probability,
    shape = verb_type
  )
) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(color = "#1F5A85", size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~contentfulness) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Probability at zero random effects",
    y = "Probability averaged over random effects",
    shape = "Verb class"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Predictions for returning participants or observed lexical material may condition on their fitted deviations. Predictions for new participants or verbs cannot reuse deviations from observed groups. Every probability summary should state which target it uses.

The displayed row computes both targets for one fixed cell: `conditional_probability` applies the inverse logit at zero deviations, whereas `marginal_probability` numerically averages the same inverse link over the fitted random intercept distribution. Their difference comes from nonlinearity rather than from a different coefficient vector.

Numerals are missing on many trials, so we use the complete binary preposition response rather than conditioning on a selected duration. The analysis consequently asks about the preposition choice recorded for the represented trials.

## Recap and check

1. Does `re.form = NA` average over random effects? No. It sets deviations to zero; averaging requires the integration shown above.
2. Why are three intercepts present? They correspond to repeated participants, verbs, and sentences in the incidence table. We include them because those three kinds of unit recur, rather than because more terms are generically preferable.

We next apply the same logic to an [ordered response](ordinal-mixed-models.qmd).
